lessons.title: Ground Staff Desk
lessons.topic: Async Python, type hints and Pydantic
lessons.summary: Run many model calls at once with asyncio, keep the event loop free of blocking code, and validate replies with Pydantic models.

mentor: Each passenger here needs one call to the airline. Each call takes about a second.
We have 20 passengers and one staff member.
Before we change anything, let's see how long they wait.

question.prompt: With one staff member making calls one at a time, how long until all 20 passengers are served?
question.explain: One call at a time means 20 calls of 1 second each, back to back. The staff member spends almost all of that time just waiting for the airline to answer.

video.title: Async Python: the event loop, gather, type hints and Pydantic

sections.heading: Most of an LLM call is waiting
sections.body: A call to a model provider is a flight to Model City. Your code sends a request, then waits for the network and the provider to do the work. Your CPU does almost nothing during that second. This kind of work is called I/O-bound. With normal blocking code, the worker (the staff member at the desk) stands frozen until the answer comes back, so 20 calls take 20 seconds. The fix is not more CPU. It's letting one worker start a call, go and start the next one while the first is in the air, and come back to each answer when it lands.

sections.heading: The event loop, async and await
sections.body: asyncio gives you an event loop: a single thread that keeps a list of tasks and runs whichever one is ready. You mark a function with async def to make it a coroutine. Inside it, await means "pause this task here until the result is ready, and let the loop run other tasks meanwhile". await does not make the call faster and does not start a new thread. It just hands control back to the loop. When the network reply arrives, the loop resumes your task from the same line.
sections.code:
import asyncio

async def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # stands in for a network call
    return f"answer to {prompt}"

print(asyncio.run(ask("hello")))

sections.heading: Running calls together with asyncio.gather
sections.body: asyncio.gather takes many coroutines, runs them on the loop at the same time, and returns their results in the same order you passed them in. Twenty one-second calls now finish in about one second. In real systems you rarely want unlimited concurrency: the provider has rate limits, so you cap how many flights are in the air with an asyncio.Semaphore. If one task raises, gather raises too unless you pass return_exceptions=True and handle each result yourself.

sections.heading: One blocking call freezes the whole desk
sections.body: The event loop is one thread. If any task runs code that blocks, such as time.sleep(5), requests.get(), a sync database driver or a long CPU loop, the loop cannot switch to anything else. Every request on that loop stops, including your health check. This is the most common async bug in production. Use async versions of libraries (asyncio.sleep, httpx.AsyncClient, asyncpg). If you must call blocking code, move it off the loop with await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...). Heavy CPU work belongs in a separate process or worker.

sections.heading: Type hints
sections.body: Type hints describe what a function takes and returns: def fetch_all(prompts: list[str]) -> list[Reply]. Python does not check them when the code runs. Tools like mypy or pyright check them before you ship, and your editor uses them for autocomplete. On a team, and especially when a coding agent writes part of the code, hints act as a contract that a tool can verify. They catch things like passing a dict where a Reply is expected, or forgetting that a value can be None (write it as str | None).

sections.heading: Pydantic models for replies and settings
sections.body: A model provider returns JSON, and JSON can be missing fields or have the wrong types. A Pydantic model checks the shape at runtime and gives you a typed object, or raises a ValidationError that says exactly what was wrong. Validate at the edge, right after the call returns, so the rest of your code can trust the data. The same idea works for settings: pydantic-settings reads environment variables into a typed Settings object and fails at startup if one is missing.

keyPoints: LLM calls are I/O-bound: the time goes to waiting, so run them concurrently.
await pauses the current task and lets the event loop run others.
asyncio.gather runs many calls together; a Semaphore caps how many at once.
One blocking call on the event loop freezes every request on it.
Use type hints for tools and Pydantic to validate data at runtime.

questions.prompt: What does await do?
options: It pauses this task and lets the event loop run others
It runs the call in a new thread
questions.explain: await hands control back to the event loop until the result is ready. The call itself takes just as long, and no new thread is created.

questions.prompt: A slow time.sleep(5) inside an async handler will…
options: block every request on that event loop
questions.explain: time.sleep blocks the single thread the event loop runs on, so nothing else can run for 5 seconds. Only asyncio.sleep yields to other tasks.

questions.prompt: Why use a Pydantic model for model replies?
options: To validate the shape and types before using them
To store replies in a database
questions.explain: Pydantic checks the JSON you got back against the fields and types you expect, and fails loudly if they don't match. It has no effect on speed or storage.

steps.upgrade: The desk gets an extra screen showing live concurrent calls, and staff handle many passengers smoothly.

review.prompt: You have 200 prompts and the provider allows about 10 requests at once. What do you put around your gathered calls?
options: An asyncio.Semaphore(10) so only 10 calls run at a time
review.explain: gather starts everything at once, so you need a Semaphore to cap it. time.sleep would block the event loop and make things worse.

review.prompt: What happens if you call a function with the wrong type for a parameter that has a type hint?
options: Python raises a TypeError straight away
The code runs faster because of the hint
Python runs it anyway; a checker like mypy or pyright would have flagged it
review.explain: Type hints aren't enforced when the code runs. Static checkers catch the mismatch before you ship, and Pydantic is what you use when you need runtime checks.

lessons.title: Check-in & Document Check
lessons.summary: Build a FastAPI endpoint that validates requests at the door, uses the right status codes, and returns one consistent error format.

mentor: Thirty passengers are on their way. Some have bad paperwork.
Right now one bad document shuts the counter for everyone.
Let's find out why before we fix anything.

question.prompt: A request is missing a required field. What should the API return?
options: A 422 with a message naming the missing field
question.explain: The problem is the client's request, so it gets a 4xx code that names the field to fix. A 500 says your server broke, and a 200 hides the problem.

video.title: FastAPI: request models, validation, status codes and error contracts

sections.heading: Routes and request models
sections.body: In FastAPI, a route is a function tied to a method and a path, like POST /chat. This is the check-in counter. Instead of reading raw JSON by hand, you declare a Pydantic model as the parameter type. FastAPI parses the body, validates it against the model, and only calls your function if it passes. Your handler receives a typed object, so it never has to check whether a field exists. You can also declare a response_model so the output is checked and documented too.

sections.heading: Validation happens at the door
sections.body: When a body doesn't match the model, FastAPI rejects it before your code runs and returns a 422 with details: which field, and what was wrong (missing, wrong type, too long). This is the document check. Bad paperwork is turned away with a slip, and the counter stays open for the next passenger. Use Field constraints for limits such as min_length, max_length, ge and le, and Literal or Enum types for fixed choices. The more you encode in the model, the less defensive code you need inside the handler.

sections.heading: Status codes that tell the truth
sections.body: Clients decide what to do from the status code, so pick it carefully. 400: the request is malformed in a general way. 401: we don't know who you are (missing or bad credentials). 403: we know who you are, but you aren't allowed to do this. 404: the thing you asked for doesn't exist. 422: the request is well-formed JSON, but the fields fail validation. 429: you're sending too much, or you're over quota, so slow down. 500: our code broke. A 4xx means the client should change something; a 5xx means we should.

sections.heading: One error contract everywhere
sections.body: If /chat returns {"detail": ...}, /upload returns {"msg": ...} and the proxy returns HTML, every client needs special-case parsing. Pick one shape and use it for every error, for example {"error": {"code": "prompt_too_long", "message": "..."}}. The code is a stable string that programs can switch on. The message is for humans. In FastAPI you get this by registering exception handlers, including one for validation errors, so even the built-in 422s follow your contract.

sections.heading: Limit input size at the boundary
sections.body: An LLM API has a cost that grows with input. A 2 MB prompt can blow your context window, cost real money (a few hundred rupees per call adds up fast), and tie up a worker for a long time. Reject oversize input at your API boundary, before anything reaches the model. Use max_length on text fields, cap the number of items in lists, and set a body-size limit at the proxy or server (413 Payload Too Large). If precision matters, count tokens rather than characters before sending the call.

sections.heading: Never let one bad request close the counter
sections.body: A 500 should mean a real bug, not a bad input. If your handler raises KeyError on an odd payload, that's a missing validation rule. For the bugs you didn't predict, add a catch-all exception handler: log the full error with the request ID, and return a generic 500 in your standard shape without a stack trace. Stack traces leak internals and help attackers. The key property is that one failure affects one request. The next passenger in the queue still gets served.

keyPoints: Declare request models so FastAPI validates input before your code runs.
4xx means the client must change something; 5xx means your server failed.
429 is for rate limits and quotas, 422 for invalid fields, 401/403 for auth.
Use one error shape, {error: {code, message}}, on every endpoint.
Limit prompt size at the API boundary, before calling the model.

questions.prompt: A client sends a valid request but has hit their quota. Best status?
questions.explain: 429 tells the client to slow down or wait. A 500 would wrongly blame your server, and 404 means the resource doesn't exist.

questions.prompt: Why keep one error format across all endpoints?
options: Clients can handle errors the same way everywhere
questions.explain: One shape means one piece of error-handling code in every client. FastAPI doesn't require it; you set it up with exception handlers.

questions.prompt: Where should prompt length be limited?
options: At the API boundary, before calling the model
questions.explain: Checking at the boundary rejects bad input cheaply and clearly. If you leave it to the model, you've already paid for the call and get a vague provider error back.

steps.upgrade: The counter shows a clean document-check scanner and rejection slips, and the queue never stops.

review.prompt: A request has a valid API key, but that user isn't allowed to use this workspace. Which status fits?
review.explain: 403 means "we know who you are, but you can't do this". 401 is for missing or invalid credentials, and this user has valid ones.

review.prompt: Your handler raises KeyError on an unexpected payload, and the client gets a 500 with a Python stack trace. Best fix?
options: Keep the stack trace so clients can debug
Validate with a request model so bad input gets a 422, and return a generic error body for real bugs
review.explain: Bad input is the client's problem and deserves a clear 4xx. A stack trace leaks internals, and a 200 hides the failure.

lessons.title: Gate Announcements
lessons.summary: Stream model output to users with SSE so the first words appear in under a second, and cancel upstream work when they leave.

mentor: Passengers think the gate is broken when it's silent for eight seconds.
And we keep paying for work after people have left.
Two problems, one gate. Let's watch it first.

question.prompt: The full answer takes 8 s to generate. With streaming, when does the user see the first words?
question.explain: The model produces tokens one by one, and the first ones are usually ready in well under a second. Streaming sends them as they arrive instead of waiting for the last one.

video.title: Streaming LLM output: SSE, websockets and cancelling on disconnect

sections.heading: Time to first token
sections.body: An LLM generates its answer one token at a time. A long answer may take 8 seconds in total, but the first token is often ready in 300 to 800 ms. If your API waits for the whole answer before replying (buffering), the user stares at a silent gate for 8 seconds and assumes it's broken. Two numbers matter: time to first token (TTFT), which shapes how fast the product feels, and total generation time, which shapes how long a worker stays busy. Streaming improves the first one and leaves the second unchanged.

sections.heading: Server-sent events (SSE)
sections.body: SSE is a simple, one-way stream from server to client over normal HTTP. The response has Content-Type text/event-stream and stays open. Each message is a line starting with "data:" followed by a blank line. Browsers support it with EventSource, it passes through most proxies, and it fits the shape of chat: the client sends one request, then the server talks. In FastAPI you return a StreamingResponse wrapping an async generator.
sections.code:
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

async def token_events(prompt: str):
    async for token in model.stream(prompt):
        yield f"data: {token}\n\n"
    yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"

@app.post("/chat/stream")
async def chat_stream(req: ChatRequest):
    return StreamingResponse(token_events(req.prompt),
                             media_type="text/event-stream")

sections.heading: When to use websockets instead
sections.body: A websocket is a long-lived, two-way connection. Both sides can send messages at any time. That matters when the user needs to talk while the model is talking: voice assistants, live interruption, collaborative editing, or real-time agents that ask for input mid-task. The cost is more operational work, including sticky connections, custom reconnect logic, load balancer settings and auth on upgrade. For ordinary text chat where the client asks once and the server streams back, SSE is simpler and usually enough.

sections.heading: Streaming through your API, end to end
sections.body: To stream, every hop must pass data on as it arrives. Ask the provider for a streamed response, read it with an async iterator, and yield each chunk to the client straight away. Don't collect chunks in a list first, or you've rebuilt buffering. A common surprise: it streams locally, but in production the user gets everything at once. Usually a reverse proxy or load balancer is buffering. For nginx, turn off proxy_buffering for that route or send the header X-Accel-Buffering: no.

sections.heading: Detecting disconnects and cancelling upstream work
sections.body: When a passenger walks away mid-announcement, the crew should stop. If the user closes the tab and you keep reading from the provider, you pay for every token nobody will read, and you keep a worker and a provider slot busy. Check whether the client is still connected while streaming, and when it isn't, stop the generator and close the upstream stream. Closing the provider's stream (or cancelling the task) tells the provider to stop generating.
sections.code:
from fastapi import Request

async def token_events(request: Request, prompt: str):
    stream = await model.open_stream(prompt)
    try:
        async for token in stream:
            if await request.is_disconnected():
                break
            yield f"data: {token}\n\n"
    finally:
        await stream.aclose()  # stop upstream generation

sections.heading: What streaming doesn't change
sections.body: Streaming doesn't make the model faster, change the answer, or use fewer tokens. It changes when the user sees progress. It also changes how errors work. Once you've sent a 200 and the first tokens, you can't change the status code. If the provider fails halfway, send an error event in your stream (for example data: {"error": {"code": "upstream_failed"}}) so the client can show a message and offer a retry. Log the partial answer length and the reason, so you can see how often this happens.

keyPoints: Time to first token shapes how fast it feels; streaming cuts it to under a second.
SSE is one-way over HTTP and fits text chat; websockets are for two-way, like voice.
Every hop, including proxies, must pass chunks on without buffering.
On client disconnect, stop and close the upstream stream, or you pay for unread tokens.
After streaming starts, report failures as an error event, not a status code.

questions.prompt: Main benefit of streaming to the user?
options: They see progress almost at once
questions.explain: Streaming shows the first words while the rest is still being generated. The answer and the token count are the same as without streaming.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer websockets over SSE?
options: When both sides need to send messages continuously, like voice
questions.explain: Websockets are two-way, which matters when the user speaks or interrupts during the answer. For plain text answers, SSE is simpler and enough.

questions.prompt: If the user closes the tab mid-answer and you don't cancel…
options: you keep paying for tokens nobody reads
the answer is saved for later
questions.explain: The provider keeps generating as long as your server keeps the stream open. Nothing stops it or saves the answer unless you build that.

steps.upgrade: The gate gets a live announcement board, and walk-aways no longer cost anything.

review.prompt: Streaming works on your laptop, but in production users see the whole answer arrive at once. Most likely cause?
options: The model stopped streaming in production
A reverse proxy or load balancer is buffering the response
review.explain: Proxies like nginx buffer responses by default, which holds chunks until the end. Turn off buffering for the streaming route.

review.prompt: The provider fails halfway through a streamed answer. You've already sent status 200. What do you do?
options: Do nothing; the client will notice the gap
Send an error event in the stream so the client can show it and offer a retry
review.explain: Headers, including the status, are already sent and can't change. An explicit error event is the only clear signal the client gets.

lessons.title: Rebooking Desk
lessons.topic: Background jobs, retries, timeouts and idempotency
lessons.summary: Make model calls survive a slow or failing provider with timeouts, safe retries with jittered backoff, background jobs and idempotency keys.

mentor: Model City is having a slow night. For about ten seconds, many flights take 15 seconds instead of 1.
Our gates wait for every plane, however long it takes.
Passengers give up after 10 seconds. Watch what happens.

question.prompt: Model City slows down for ten seconds. What happens at our gates?
options: Only the passengers on slow flights are affected
All gates get stuck waiting, the queue grows, and passengers leave
Nothing much; it recovers on its own
question.explain: Every slow flight holds a gate. After a few seconds all 10 gates are holding slow planes, so even passengers whose flights would be fast can't get a gate.

video.title: Timeouts, retries, backoff with jitter, background jobs and idempotency keys

sections.heading: Timeouts: stop waiting forever
sections.body: Many HTTP clients wait a long time, or forever, by default. When the provider has a slow patch, each slow call holds one of your workers (a gate). With 10 workers and enough slow calls, all 10 are stuck, and fast requests queue behind them. A timeout gives up after a set time and frees the worker. Base it on real latency: if p99 is 1.5 s, a 2 s timeout cuts off only the stuck ones. Remember the catch: a timeout frees your worker, not the provider. The provider is still working on the abandoned request, and it still counts against your rate limit.

sections.heading: Which errors deserve a retry
sections.body: Retry only when the next attempt might succeed. Timeouts and connection errors are often temporary, because the next flight may be fast. 429 Too Many Requests means "wait and try again"; if it has a Retry-After header, wait at least that long. 5xx errors (500, 502, 503, 504) are usually temporary provider trouble. Never retry 400, 401, 403, 404 or 422. The request itself is wrong, and sending it again gets the same answer while adding load. Fix the request instead.

sections.heading: Exponential backoff with full jitter
sections.body: Retrying instantly hits the provider again at its worst moment. Exponential backoff waits longer after each failure: about 0.5 s, then 1 s, then 2 s, with a cap. Jitter adds randomness so that a thousand clients that failed together don't all retry together. With full jitter you pick a random wait between zero and the backoff value. That spreads retries evenly and gives the provider room to recover. Always cap attempts; three retries is a common limit.

sections.heading: Retry storms and retry budgets
sections.body: Retries add load. If each request may try 4 times, a bad minute can send up to 4 times the normal traffic to a provider that is already struggling. Add the abandoned requests still running after timeouts, and you pass the provider's capacity, so the control tower turns red with 429s. That's a retry storm: your own retries keep the outage going. Prevent it with a retry budget. Cap attempts per request, and cap retries across all traffic (for example, retries may be at most 10% of calls). When the budget is spent, fail fast. A circuit breaker does the same at a larger scale.

sections.heading: Background jobs for long work
sections.body: Some work shouldn't happen inside the HTTP request at all: a report that takes 90 seconds, a batch of 500 summaries, or anything that needs several model calls in a row. Put it on a queue (the baggage belt). Return 202 Accepted with a job ID straight away, and let a separate worker process the job, with its own timeouts and retries. The client polls GET /jobs/{id} or receives a webhook. Queues also absorb bursts: when passengers arrive faster than gates can serve them, jobs wait in line instead of being dropped.

sections.heading: Idempotency keys: safe to retry
sections.body: A refund call times out. Did the refund happen? You can't tell. Maybe the provider finished just after you gave up. If you retry blindly, the customer may get ₹2,000 refunded twice. An idempotency key fixes this. Generate a unique key once per logical operation (the boarding-pass number) and send the same key on every attempt. The server stores the key with its result, and a repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of doing the work again. Reads like "fetch order status" are naturally safe to retry. Anything that charges, refunds, sends or creates needs a key.

keyPoints: Always set a timeout; it frees your worker, but the provider keeps working.
Retry timeouts, 429 and 5xx; never retry 400-type errors.
Use exponential backoff with full jitter, and cap attempts with a retry budget.
Move long work to background jobs on a queue and return a job ID.
Send the same idempotency key on every attempt of an operation with side effects.

questions.prompt: Why add random jitter to backoff?
options: So many clients don't retry at the same moment
questions.explain: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together and hit the provider in waves. Jitter spreads them out, and it doesn't make any single retry faster.

questions.prompt: Which is safe to retry without an idempotency key?
questions.explain: Reading status has no side effects, so doing it twice is harmless. Charging or refunding twice moves money twice.

questions.prompt: The provider returns 400 Bad Request. You should…
questions.explain: A 400 means the request itself is wrong, so every retry fails the same way and adds load. Backoff helps only with temporary errors.

steps.upgrade: The rebooking desk gets a "Retry policy v2" sign; planes leave in gentle, spread-out waves, and the tower light stays green during later disruptions.

review.prompt: Your client times out a model call after 2 s. What is true about the provider at that moment?
options: It stops working on the request straight away
It may still be processing it, and it still counts against your rate limit
It refunds the tokens for that request
review.explain: A client timeout only frees your worker. The provider doesn't know you gave up, so the request keeps using its capacity until it finishes.

review.prompt: A user-facing report takes about 90 seconds to generate. Best design?
options: Hold the HTTP request open for 90 s
Raise the client timeout to 5 minutes
Queue it as a background job, return 202 with a job ID, and let the client poll or be notified
review.explain: Long requests tie up workers and break on any network hiccup. A queued job has its own retries, and the client can check back.

lessons.title: Cargo Container Bay
lessons.summary: Write a Dockerfile that rebuilds in seconds, keeps secrets out of every layer, and reads config from the environment.

mentor: Every small change takes four minutes to rebuild.
And security says something sensitive is inside our container.
Let's open it up and look at the layers.

question.prompt: You change one line of app code. With COPY . . before pip install, what rebuilds?
options: The install layer and everything after it
question.explain: COPY . . includes your code, so a one-line change breaks the cache at that step. Every step after it, including the slow pip install, runs again.

video.title: Docker: layers, caching, slim images, config and secrets

sections.heading: Images and layers
sections.body: A Docker image is a stack of read-only layers, like a cargo container packed in layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile (FROM, COPY, RUN) adds one layer on top of the last. A running container is the image plus a thin writable layer. Layers are stored and shared by content, so two images built on the same base share those bytes. This makes images efficient, and it also means that whatever goes into a layer stays there, even if a later layer seems to remove it.

sections.heading: Layer caching and Dockerfile order
sections.body: When you rebuild, Docker reuses a cached layer if the instruction and its inputs haven't changed. At the first step that has changed, the cache breaks, and every step after it runs again. So order steps from least to most frequently changed. Copy only requirements.txt first, install dependencies, then copy your source code. A code change then only rebuilds the last cheap layer, and the slow install stays cached.
sections.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

sections.heading: Slim base images and .dockerignore
sections.body: The full python image is about a gigabyte and carries compilers and tools you don't need at runtime. python:3.12-slim is a fraction of that. It pulls faster, starts faster, and has fewer packages that need security patches. The build context is everything Docker sends to the builder, and COPY . . will copy all of it. A .dockerignore file keeps out what doesn't belong: Git history, virtualenvs, caches, local data and, most importantly, .env files.

sections.heading: Config from environment variables
sections.body: Build one image and run it everywhere: dev, staging and production. What changes between them (database URL, model name, log level, API keys) comes from environment variables at runtime, not from the image. pydantic-settings makes this typed and strict: it reads the variables, converts types, and refuses to start if a required one is missing. That's better than finding out at 2 a.m. when the first request fails.
sections.code:
from pydantic import SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    database_url: str
    model_name: str = "small-model"
    llm_api_key: SecretStr  # hidden when printed or logged

settings = Settings()  # reads DATABASE_URL, MODEL_NAME, LLM_API_KEY

sections.heading: Secrets never go in images
sections.body: If a .env file or API key is copied into any layer, it's in the image for good. A later RUN rm .env adds a new layer that hides the file, but the earlier layer still contains it, and anyone who can pull the image can extract it. Registries get shared, cached and leaked. Pass secrets at runtime through environment variables from your platform or a secret manager. If a build step needs a secret (for example a private package index), use BuildKit's --mount=type=secret so it never lands in a layer. If a key was ever baked in, rotate it first, then rebuild.

keyPoints: Each Dockerfile instruction is a layer; a change rebuilds that layer and all after it.
Copy requirements and install before copying source code.
Use a slim base image and a .dockerignore that excludes .env and .git.
Read config from environment variables with typed settings.
Secrets in any layer stay there; pass them at runtime and rotate any leaked key.

questions.prompt: Best place for an API key at runtime?
options: An environment variable or secret manager
questions.explain: Runtime injection keeps the key out of the image and out of history. Anything in an image or repo is copied to every machine and person that touches it.

questions.prompt: Why copy requirements.txt before the source code?
options: So the install layer is cached when only code changes
questions.explain: Dependencies change rarely and code changes often, so installing first keeps the slow step cached. The image ends up the same size either way.

questions.prompt: Deleting a secret in a later layer…
options: doesn't remove it; it's still in the earlier layer
questions.explain: Layers are read-only. The deletion only hides the file in the final view, and the earlier layer still holds it.

steps.upgrade: The containers are neatly stacked with a green "scanned" seal, and rebuilds are fast.

review.prompt: You find a live API key baked into an image that was pushed to your registry last week. What do you do first?
options: Rebuild the image without the key and push it
Delete the image tag from the registry
review.explain: The key may already have been copied, so only rotating it makes it useless. Rebuilding and deleting tags are cleanup steps that come after.

review.prompt: Why use python:3.12-slim instead of python:3.12 as the base?
options: It has a newer Python version
It's much smaller with fewer packages, so pulls are faster and there's less to patch
review.explain: Both have the same Python version. Slim drops build tools and extras you don't need at runtime.

lessons.title: Maintenance Hangar
lessons.topic: Git, code review, CI and pytest
lessons.summary: Review a change, including agent-written code, for edge cases and side effects, and back it with focused, non-flaky tests that CI enforces.

mentor: A coding agent made this change. It looks fine and the demo works.
Review it before it flies.
I'll tell you now: there's more than one problem in there.

question.prompt: The change passes the demo. Is that enough to ship?
options: No; it needs tests and review for cases the demo didn't cover
Yes, if the agent says it tested it
question.explain: A demo shows the happy path once. Missing null checks, double calls and flaky behaviour only show up in tests and careful review.

video.title: Pull requests, reviewing diffs, pytest, CI gates and flaky tests

sections.heading: Branches and pull requests
sections.body: Keep main always deployable. Each change happens on its own branch and arrives as a pull request: the diff, a description of why, and automated checks. Small PRs get real reviews, while a 2,000-line PR gets a skim and a "looks good". Write the description for the reviewer: what changed, why, how you tested it, and what you're unsure about. The PR is the plane rolling into the hangar. It doesn't fly until the checklist passes and someone has inspected it.

sections.heading: Reviewing a diff, especially agent-written code
sections.body: Coding agents write plausible code fast, and plausible isn't the same as correct. Review behaviour before style. Ask what happens with None, an empty list, a huge input or a slow dependency. Look for side effects such as writes, payments, emails and external calls, and ask whether they can happen twice. A retry wrapped around a non-idempotent call is a classic bug. Check error handling: is anything swallowed silently? Treat "I tested it" from an agent as a claim to verify, not evidence. Then ask what the demo didn't cover, and make sure a test covers it.

sections.heading: Focused tests with pytest
sections.body: A good test checks one behaviour, has a clear name, and fails for one reason. Use a fake in place of the real model client so the test is fast, free and repeatable, and so you can count calls or force errors. Test the edge cases you found in review. Each test should fail on the buggy version and pass on the fixed one. That's how you know it actually guards something.
sections.code:
import pytest

class FakeModel:
    def __init__(self, reply):
        self.reply, self.calls = reply, 0
    async def generate(self, prompt):
        self.calls += 1
        return self.reply

async def test_none_reply_returns_fallback():
    model = FakeModel(reply=None)
    assert await answer(model, "hi") == "Sorry, try again."

async def test_refund_is_called_once():
    model = FakeModel(reply="ok")
    await refund(model, order_id="A1")
    assert model.calls == 1

sections.heading: Fixtures
sections.body: pytest fixtures provide the setup a test needs, such as a fake client, a temporary database or fixed settings, by naming it as a parameter. They keep tests short and make setup consistent. A fixture can clean up after itself with yield. Keep fixtures simple and local. If a test needs five fixtures and a page of setup, the code under test is probably doing too much. (Async tests like the ones above need a plugin such as pytest-asyncio or anyio.)

sections.heading: CI pipelines that block merges
sections.body: Continuous integration runs your checks on every push and PR: install, lint, type check (mypy or pyright) and tests. Its value comes from blocking. Turn on branch protection so a PR can't merge into main unless the required checks are green and a reviewer has approved. CI that only reports is ignored within a week. Keep the pipeline fast, ideally a few minutes, so people don't look for ways around it. Style opinions belong to an auto-formatter, not to review comments.

sections.heading: Flaky tests
sections.body: A flaky test passes sometimes and fails sometimes on the same code. The usual causes are randomness, real time (sleeps and clocks), network calls, test order, and shared state between tests. Re-running until green teaches the team to ignore red, which is worse than having no test. Find the source and control it. Seed the random generator, inject a fake clock or a sleep function, replace the network with a fake, and give each test its own data. If you must quarantine a test, do it with a ticket and an owner, never silently.

keyPoints: A demo proves the happy path once; tests and review cover the rest.
Review agent code for edge cases and side effects before style.
Write focused tests with fakes that fail on the bug and pass on the fix.
CI must block merges on failing tests and checks.
Fix flaky tests by controlling randomness and time, never by re-running.

questions.prompt: A test passes 9 times in 10. Best response?
options: Find the source of randomness or timing and remove it
questions.explain: Flakiness has a cause, usually randomness, time or shared state, and controlling it makes the test trustworthy. Re-running hides the problem, and deleting it removes the guard.

questions.prompt: What should CI block on?
questions.explain: Blocking on objective checks stops broken code reaching main. Informational CI soon gets ignored.

questions.prompt: Reviewing agent-written code, focus first on…
options: behaviour in edge cases and side effects
questions.explain: Bugs that hurt users come from behaviour: nulls, double calls and missing error handling. Naming and comments matter much less.

steps.upgrade: The hangar shows a green CI light and an inspection stamp on approved planes.

review.prompt: A test checks that a retry waits about 1 second, using real time.sleep and time.time. It fails now and then on CI. Best fix?
options: Inject a fake clock or sleep function so the test controls time
review.explain: Real time depends on machine load, so the test can never be fully reliable. A fake clock makes it exact and instant, while a bigger tolerance only makes it fail less often.

review.prompt: Why use a fake model client in unit tests instead of calling the real API?
options: Python tests can't make network calls
Fakes find more bugs inside the provider
Tests run fast, cost nothing, give the same result every time, and can simulate failures
review.explain: Fakes give you control and repeatability, such as forcing a 429 or counting calls. Real calls are slow, cost money and vary between runs.

lessons.title: Passenger Records Office
lessons.summary: Read a Postgres query plan, add the right index without locking the table, run migrations safely, and size a connection pool.

mentor: Support needs one customer's chat history. It takes 9 seconds.
And tonight we need to add a column to that same table.
Let's look at what the database is actually doing.

question.prompt: Finding one customer's chats in a million rows with no index means…
options: It jumps straight to the rows
The database reads most of the table
question.explain: Without an index there's no catalogue, so Postgres does a sequential scan and checks every row. The cache can make reads cheaper, but it doesn't avoid reading them.

video.title: Postgres essentials: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, indexes, safe migrations and pools

sections.heading: Tables and keys
sections.body: Each table holds rows with a fixed set of typed columns. A primary key uniquely identifies a row, and Postgres indexes it automatically. A foreign key links a row to a row in another table and stops orphans, but Postgres doesn't index foreign key columns for you. In an AI app, a typical table stores conversations or messages, and you almost always fetch them for one customer, newest first. That access pattern should drive your indexes.

sections.heading: Reading a plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
sections.body: EXPLAIN shows the plan Postgres intends to use. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows each step with real row counts and timings. Look for Seq Scan on a big table (the clerk walking every shelf), and compare estimated rows with actual rows. Big gaps mean stale statistics. Because ANALYZE runs the query, wrap writes in BEGIN … ROLLBACK when you test them.
sections.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, created_at, content
FROM conversations
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
-- before: Seq Scan on conversations ... actual time=...9000 ms
-- after:  Index Scan using conversations_customer_created_idx ... 0.4 ms

sections.heading: Indexes and when they help
sections.body: A B-tree index is the catalogue: a sorted structure that leads straight to matching rows. It helps when a query picks a small share of rows (one customer out of a million), and it can also return rows already sorted. A composite index on (customer_id, created_at) serves WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 in one pass. Column order matters. The index works for queries that filter on the leftmost column, not for created_at alone. Indexes aren't free: each one slows inserts and updates and takes disk space, so add them for real queries, not just in case.

sections.heading: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
sections.body: A plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes to the table for as long as it takes to build, which can be minutes on a large table. At peak, every insert queues behind it. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY builds the index while reads and writes continue. It's slower and does more work, it can't run inside a transaction block, and if it fails it leaves an INVALID index that you must drop and build again. On a production table, this is the default choice.

sections.heading: Safe migrations
sections.body: Most ALTER TABLE statements need a strong lock, even if only briefly. If a long query is running, the ALTER waits for it, and every new query then waits behind the ALTER, so the office closes. Set a lock_timeout so the migration gives up instead of blocking everyone, then retry. Know which changes rewrite the whole table: changing a column's type, or adding a column with a volatile default. Since Postgres 11, adding a column with a constant default is a quick metadata change. For big changes use expand and contract: add a nullable column, backfill in small batches, then add the constraint.

sections.heading: Connection pools
sections.body: Each Postgres connection is a separate server process using memory, and max_connections is often around 100. An async API with 500 requests in flight can't give each one its own connection. A pool keeps a small set of open connections and lends them out briefly. Use your driver's pool (asyncpg, SQLAlchemy) and, at scale, PgBouncer in front of Postgres. The key rule for AI apps: never hold a connection while you await a model call. A 6-second flight to Model City with a connection checked out will drain the pool, and everything else waits.

keyPoints: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the real plan and timings; look for Seq Scan on big tables.
Composite indexes follow your query: filter column first, then sort column.
Build indexes on live tables with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
Use lock_timeout and expand-and-contract for migrations at scale.
Pool connections and never hold one across a model call.

questions.prompt: An index on conversations(customer_id, created_at) helps…
questions.explain: It matches a query that filters by customer and sorts by time. It doesn't help unrelated queries, and it makes inserts slightly slower.

questions.prompt: Adding a column with a default on a huge table at peak time…
options: can lock or slow the table; plan it safely
questions.explain: Depending on the default and the Postgres version, it can rewrite the table or wait on a lock that queues every query. Even fast changes need a lock, so use lock_timeout and choose the timing.

questions.prompt: What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE show?
options: The plan the database used and how long each step took
questions.explain: It runs the query and reports the actual plan, row counts and time for each step. For schema and sizes you'd use \d and the size functions.

steps.upgrade: The records office gets a catalogue cabinet; lookups are instant, and renovations happen at night with the office open.

review.prompt: You have an index on conversations(customer_id, created_at). Which query can NOT use it well?
options: WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC
WHERE created_at > now() - interval '1 day' (all customers)
review.explain: A composite index is sorted by its leftmost column first, so filtering only on created_at can't jump to the rows. Both queries on customer_id can use it.

review.prompt: Your handler takes a pooled DB connection, then awaits a 6 s model call before releasing it. What happens at peak?
options: The pool runs dry and other requests wait for a connection
Postgres speeds up because connections are reused
review.explain: Each connection sits idle for 6 seconds while the model call is in flight, so a small pool is used up quickly. Release the connection before the model call.

lessons.title: Control Tower Room
lessons.summary: Add request IDs and structured JSON logs, record errors with context, and use rate, errors and duration to find a failing step fast.

mentor: A customer says her chat failed at 2:13 a.m.
Find out why. You have five minutes.
Here are the logs. Good luck.

question.prompt: Logs are plain text with no request IDs. How easy is it to find one customer's failed request among 50,000 lines?
options: Very hard; many requests happened at the same moment
question.explain: Dozens of requests share the same minute, and their lines are mixed together. You can't tell which line belongs to her, though it isn't strictly impossible with enough time.

video.title: Observability: JSON logs, request IDs, traces and RED metrics

sections.heading: Structured JSON logs
sections.body: A plain-text log line is written for a human reading one line. In production you search millions of lines, so write logs as data: one JSON object per line with consistent field names. Your log tool can then filter by any field (request_id, customer_id, status, step) instead of relying on a fragile text search. Use a standard set of fields everywhere, and add event-specific ones as needed.

sections.heading: Request IDs and trace IDs
sections.body: Every passenger carries a flight number. Generate a request ID at the edge of your system, when the request first arrives, or accept one from an incoming X-Request-ID header. Attach it to every log line for that request, return it in the response headers, and pass it on in calls to other services and the model provider. Across several services, a trace ID (the W3C traceparent header) ties all the hops together. Show the ID in the error message users see, and support can then find the exact request in seconds.

sections.heading: Middleware that sets the ID once
sections.body: Don't pass the request ID by hand through every function. FastAPI middleware can set it once per request, and Python's contextvars keeps it available anywhere in that request's async code. A logging filter or formatter then adds it to every line automatically. The middleware below also returns the ID in the response header and logs one summary line per request with status and duration. When you call the model provider, read request_id.get() and send it as a header, so the provider's logs and yours can be matched later.
sections.code:
import time, uuid, logging
from contextvars import ContextVar
from fastapi import Request

request_id: ContextVar[str] = ContextVar("request_id", default="-")
log = logging.getLogger("api")

@app.middleware("http")
async def add_request_id(request: Request, call_next):
    rid = request.headers.get("x-request-id") or uuid.uuid4().hex
    request_id.set(rid)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["x-request-id"] = rid
    log.info("request_done", extra={"request_id": rid,
             "status": response.status_code,
             "duration_ms": round((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000)})
    return response

sections.heading: Log levels
sections.body: Levels let you control volume and urgency. DEBUG is detail for local work and is usually off in production. INFO is normal events worth keeping, such as a request completing or a job starting. WARNING means something odd happened but was handled, like a retry that succeeded. ERROR means a request failed and someone may need to look. Production usually runs at INFO. Don't log every streamed token or every loop step. Volume costs money and buries the lines you need at 2 a.m.

sections.heading: Errors with context, without secrets
sections.body: An error line that says only "error" is useless. Include what you need to act on it: request ID, the step that failed (validate, call_model, save), the status code, the attempt number, duration, and the model or provider used. Log the exception type and message, with the stack trace for real bugs. Never log passwords, API keys, tokens, card numbers or Aadhaar numbers. Be careful with full prompts and responses, since they often contain personal data. Log their length or a redacted version instead.

sections.heading: Rate, errors, duration and following a trace
sections.body: Three metrics cover most services. Rate is requests per second. Errors is the share of requests that fail. Duration is latency, watched as percentiles such as p50, p95 and p99, because averages hide the slow tail. Dashboards and alerts on these tell you that something is wrong. Logs and traces tell you why. A trace shows one request as a tree of timed spans: API, validation, database, model call and retries. OpenTelemetry is the common standard for producing them, and it lets you follow one passenger from the entrance to Model City and back.

keyPoints: Log JSON, one object per line, with consistent field names.
Generate a request ID at the edge and put it on every log line and outgoing call.
Error logs need request ID, step, status and duration, never secrets.
Rate, errors and duration are the three core service metrics; watch p95 and p99.
Metrics tell you something is wrong; traces and logs tell you where and why.

questions.prompt: Why put a request ID on every log line?
options: To follow one request across services
questions.explain: The ID ties together every line, in every service, that belongs to one request. It makes logs slightly longer, not shorter.

questions.prompt: Which belongs in an error log?
questions.explain: Context lets you find and fix the failure quickly. Passwords must never be logged, and a bare "error" tells you nothing.

questions.prompt: "Rate, errors, duration" are…
questions.explain: They're the RED metrics: how much traffic, how much fails, and how long it takes. Log levels are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING and ERROR.

steps.upgrade: The tower screens show a live trace view, and daily disruptions start here: click the alert and the camera flies to the affected station.

review.prompt: Error rate is flat, but users say chat feels slow at night. Which metric shows the problem?
options: Duration percentiles such as p95 and p99
review.explain: Slowness is a duration problem, and the tail percentiles show it even when the average looks fine. Request rate only tells you how much traffic there is.

review.prompt: Where should the request ID be created?
options: Separately in each function that logs
At the edge, when the request arrives (or taken from an incoming X-Request-ID), then passed along
review.explain: One ID created at the entrance and carried everywhere is what makes the request traceable. IDs made in several places don't link up.
